title: Norm Enforcement for AI Agents: Robustly Shaping Behavior in Multi-Agent Systems
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: Competing agents can game a reporting mechanism with false reports, so robust enforcement must cut false positives at equal detection rates.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right: agent graph, behavior examples, ROC-style plot
description: The left panel shows an example social media marketing environment. Four agents appear as emoji icons: two robots for good agents and two devils for bad agents. Each agent has a post document icon below it. Colored arrows show main actions (dark gray), rewards (dashed green), messages (blue) and reports (pink). Pink report arrows run between the agents. A gray bar of user icons at the bottom has two-way arrows to the posts. A legend sits on the far left. The middle panel uses brackets to pair good-agent and bad-agent behaviors with text. Good agents send norm-following posts and report honestly. Bad agents post violations, file false reports against competitors and send hostile messages, each with a gray italic example quote. The right panel is a plot of TPR against FPR. Colored curves show five mechanisms and a gray baseline with an error-bar marker. An arrow points to the red diamond labeled 'our best', which sits toward the ideal upper-left corner.
caption: The norm enforcement problem. Left: Agents deployed in a shared environment compete for reward. To enforce desired norms, the environment implements a mechanism that allows agents to report norm violations. However, strategic bad agents violate norms and file false reports against compliant competitors. Right: We propose five norm enforcement mechanisms and evaluate them by measuring how often they lead to removal of good (FP) vs. bad (TP) agents over time. Our best mechanism achieves half the FPR of a naive mechanism at the same level of TPR.
abstract: AI agents are increasingly deployed in shared environments where they pursue diverse goals and compete for rewards. This multi-agent competition can lead to behaviors that serve individual gains at collective cost -- for instance, marketing agents may post misleading content as a result of competing for engagement on social media. Human societies address such problems through norms that constrain acceptable behavior, supported by enforcement mechanisms that detect and penalize violations. Motivated by this, we study norm enforcement mechanisms for language model agents. We find that simple enforcement mechanisms are exploited by misaligned agents for competitive advantage, even when they are not explicitly trained or prompted to do so. We thus turn our attention to designing more robust mechanisms, and identify two key ingredients: estimating each agent's reliability over time, and updating this estimate with escalating penalties for repeated misbehavior. Across three simulated environments and a variety of agent populations, mechanisms built on these principles resist exploitation, while still penalizing norm violations at comparable or lower cost than baselines. Our results position norm enforcement mechanisms as scalable levers for shaping agents' behavior, but only when designed to anticipate becoming part of the system they govern. Our code and data are available at https://yaowenye.com/norm-enforcement.
